subject: Flight Performance and Planning
learning_objective: Calculate the CG shift when moving a load
question_text: In an aeroplane of 1,000 kg total mass, a 20 kg bag is moved from an arm of 3.0 m to an arm of 1.0 m. How does the centre of gravity change?
explanation: CG shift = mass moved x distance moved / total mass = 20 x 2.0 / 1,000 = 0.04 m, in the direction of the movement (forward).

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The bag moves forward (to a smaller arm), so the CG moves forward.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: That is out by a factor of ten.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Moving mass within the aeroplane changes the total moment and so the CG.

calculation_steps: shift = 20 kg x (3.0 - 1.0) m / 1000 kg = 0.04 m forward

subject: Flight Performance and Planning
question_text: Aerodrome elevation 2,000 ft, QNH 1003 hPa, OAT +30 degrees C. Using 30 ft per hPa and 120 ft per degree C of ISA deviation, what is the approximate density altitude?
explanation: Pressure altitude = 2,000 + (1013 - 1003) x 30 = 2,300 ft. ISA temperature there = 15 - 2 x 2.3 = 10.4 degrees C, so the deviation is +19.6 degrees C. Density altitude = 2,300 + 120 x 19.6, about 4,650 ft.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: That is the pressure altitude, without the temperature correction.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: That is the elevation, with neither correction applied.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The temperature correction uses the deviation from ISA (about +19.6 degrees C), not the full OAT of +30 degrees C.

subject: Flight Performance and Planning
question_text: What is the effect of increasing an aeroplane's mass?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lower stall speed and shorter take-off distance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Higher rate of climb because of greater momentum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Higher stall speed, longer take-off distance and lower rate of climb

choices.label: D
choices.text: No change if the CG stays within limits

explanation: More lift is needed at every speed. Stall speed rises with the square root of mass, take-off and landing distances increase, and climb performance falls.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: More mass needs more lift, so stall speed rises.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Excess power is reduced, so climb rate falls.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Mass affects performance whatever the CG position.

subject: Flight Performance and Planning
question_text: For a light aeroplane, which definition of take-off distance is normally used in flight manual performance data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The ground run only, from brake release to lift-off

choices.label: B
choices.text: The distance from lift-off to 1,000 ft

choices.label: D
choices.text: The distance from brake release to reaching a screen height of 50 ft (15 m)

explanation: Flight manual take-off distance normally includes the ground roll plus the airborne segment up to a 50 ft (15 m) screen height. It is then compared with the distance available.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The ground run is usually given separately.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Take-off distance includes the ground run and ends at the screen height.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: That is the available distance, not the required distance.

subject: Flight Performance and Planning
question_text: An aeroplane climbs at 600 ft per minute at a ground speed of 80 kt. What is its approximate climb gradient?
explanation: Horizontal speed = 80 x 6,076 / 60 = 8,101 ft per minute. Gradient = 600 / 8,101 = 0.074, i.e. 7.4 percent.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Convert ground speed to ft per minute: 80 kt is about 8,100 ft/min.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: That is out by a factor of ten.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: That would need a ground speed of about 132 kt.

subject: Flight Performance and Planning
learning_objective: Calculate time and distance to climb
question_text: An aeroplane climbs from 1,500 ft to 6,500 ft at 500 ft per minute with a ground speed of 80 kt. How far does it travel during the climb?
explanation: Height to gain = 5,000 ft. Time = 5,000 / 500 = 10 min. Distance = 80 x 10/60 = 13.3 NM.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The climb takes 10 minutes; that is the time, not the distance.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: That would correspond to a 6-minute climb.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: That would correspond to about 12.5 minutes at 80 kt.
